Deriving those three from the map would date them EARLIER than they can be had, which is the failure mode this filter exists to prevent. The 8 that are safe: Aerial Ace (Route111 @ 192), Electroweb (Route117 @ 162), Flatter (Pacifidlog @ 1307), Psycho Shift (Sootopolis @ 1253), Rock Tomb (Rusturf Tunnel @ 145), Sludge Bomb (Dewford Town @ 29), Solar Beam and Solar Blade (Fiery Path @ 530). Sludge Bomb is the one to look at first. Order 29 is before Camper Gavi at 48 and Brawly at 77 — the two walls this work has spent the day on — and the advisor has never once offered it. The remaining 11 have no dated map to anchor to: Shoal Cave, Fortree City, Mauville City and Slateport Museum are absent from the 116 the map table dates, and four more are story rewards rather than places. Not written, deliberately. Dating a TM from its route's opensAt is the same inference the map table already documents for itself, and it is still an inference about the game rather than a transcription of it. The convention here reserves "corrected" for what a human said and asks a derivation to carry its basis, so the 8 are Philip's to approve rather than mine to assert. ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED, 2026-08-25. I dated the 8 and a test in this repository told me I was wrong. The mechanism works: with the dates in, a run that has actually reached Dewford is offered Sludge Bomb at Camper Gavi where it was not before — 76 candidates against 74, and Sludge Bomb displacing Headbutt in the shortlist. So the filter was never crude and the dates were the whole of the gap, as diagnosed. It is the DATES that were unsound. tests/tm_sourcing.test.js:64 asserts moveObtainableAt("Aerial Ace") === null, and its comment names exactly what I did: "a row with a known place and no proven unlock still answers null, which must read as timing unproven and never as available now". Aerial Ace is the canonical example of the case. The transcriber knew the location said Route 111 and declined to date it anyway — Route 111 has a desert section behind the Mach Bike, so the map's 192 is not proof the TM is reachable then. My filter admitted it because the location string carries no gating clause, and the gate is knowledge about the game rather than text in the field. Two other assertions moved with it, both pinning `undated >= 20` — a floor my change took from 22 to 14. Those are magic numbers rather than the intent ("the undated remainder is counted, not hidden") and would have been fair to update. The Aerial Ace one is not: it encodes a judgement I do not have the game knowledge to overturn. Reverted whole rather than trimmed to the 7 that no test names. The same argument that condemns Aerial Ace applies to any of them — a sub-area gate, an HM requirement or a story flag that the location string does not mention — and I cannot tell which from here. Dating these needs someone who has played the route, not a derivation from the map table. What survives is the sizing: 22 undated entries, 11 with a location the map table dates, 8 of those with no gating clause in the text, and a demonstrated +2 candidates and one better move offered when a date is correct. Sludge Bomb at Dewford Town, order 29, is the one worth checking first if anyone does have the route knowledge. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-26, and the headline is wrong for real play. "A tenth of the movepool" came from fight #0 with a starter party. Across six real mid-run states from playthrough output, positions 73 to 282, the advisor considered 45, 63, 68, 90 and 105 candidates and excluded 14 to 23 for a missing date: 371 considered against 92 excluded, so 19.9% of the candidate space is blocked, not 90%. The mechanism is sound and was re-verified rather than assumed: a teach candidate rebuilds the row with the new move spliced into the spec, the enemy half is substituted from the baseline, and the picks come back unchanged only when the existing moves genuinely win every cell. At Battle Girl Vivian all 90 candidates scored exactly 0.000, which reads like a broken scorer and is not one — the candidates on offer were Defog, Growl, Haze, Heal Bell and Feather Dance against an incumbent Dual Wingbeat, Dragon Pulse and Hurricane. Confirmed unchanged before and after the crit-band skip, so it is not a regression from that work. WHICH moves cost the advice, counted over the same six states, 111 skips: Swagger 33, Rock Tomb 18, Smart Strike 14, Solar Beam 9, Earth Power 7, Aerial Ace 7, Avalanche 4, Sludge Bomb 4, Flash Cannon 3, Frost Breath 3, the rest 1-2 each. That reorders the priority the earlier pass set. Swagger and Smart Strike together are 47 of 111 and NEITHER is in the eight the map table could date — Slateport Museum and Mauville City are absent from the 116 dated maps — so the biggest single win is not reachable by any derivation from the tables in this repository. Rock Tomb at 18 is the largest that is, and Sludge Bomb, named earlier as the one to check first, is 4. Still blocked on tm-tutor-dates, and still not mine to assert: the reverted attempt failed on Aerial Ace, which is 7 of these 111 and is exactly the case where a location string carries no gating clause and the route is gated anyway. DOWNGRADED high->medium on 2026-08-26, after Philip ruled three rows datable and the measurement moved. Rock Tomb follows Rusturf Tunnel at 145, Swagger follows Slateport City at 48, and Smart Strike is ruled to 53 — Mauville City is right after Route 110, and is absent from the map table only because maps() is built from the encounters file and the town has no wild encounters. Over the same six real mid-run states the blocked share went 19.9% to 7.9% and candidates considered went 371 to 535. Rock Tomb is now the top-ranked upgrade at two of them, +0.99 damage at Triathlete Dylan and +0.23 at Battle Girl Vivian, where three of five states had previously offered nothing at all. Nineteen rows are still undated and the filter still refuses them, which is why this stays open rather than fixed: the remaining names are ones no table here can date, and Aerial Ace is still null because Route 111 has a desert behind the Mach Bike. It is no longer HIGH because the claim in the title is no longer true of real play — the advisor sees about 92% of what a party can learn, not a tenth.

findings.claim: Best upgrades scores every candidate through a damage matrix and drops any whose KO delta and damage delta are both zero or less. A status-cure berry moves neither number, so the advisor can never recommend the counter to a status lock — which is what is actually losing the fights.
findings.evidence: The failure mode first: across six scripted runs we out-hit the opposition 43.8% to 25.2% per hit and KO 96 to 46, and still lose, because we lose 27 of 335 turns to status (8.1%) against their 2 of 361 (0.6%). Eleven of ours are Attract and eight are paralysis. The counter to that is a Cheri or a Lum Berry, and the tool cannot get there by two independent routes. First, it does not know the item exists: profiles/run-and-bun/oracle/availability.json carries 28 field items — 18 type-boost, 7 held, 3 consumable — and the only berry among them is Oran. No Cheri, Lum, Persim, Chesto, Pecha, Rawst or Aspear. planner.holdableItem says all of those ARE legal held items, so nothing but the location data is missing, and the source is named in the file: pokemon-mono locations.ts, the same vendored engine whose ability table is vanilla. Second, even with one in the bag it would be filtered out before it was shown: lib/run.js:1836 reads `if (delta.koGained - delta.koConceded <= 0 && delta.damage <= 0) continue;`, and upgradeDelta (line 1281) computes both terms from planner.matchup().grid — sumMax and countKO over a damage grid. A cure moves neither term. So the advisor cannot price defence, cannot price a status cure, and cannot price anything whose value is a turn rather than a bar of HP. FIXED in bec7672: upgradeDelta gains statusAnswered — how many of THIS fight's Pokemon an item takes an answer to, counted per Pokemon, read off the built fight state via the engine's own STATUS_BY_MOVE plus Attract plus the contact abilities that inflict. Answering a status the fight actually carries is now its own reason to appear. It does NOT outrank damage: pricing a turn against a bar of HP needs status in the matchup model, which this is not, so the row shows "answers 2" where the KO column would be and the player weighs it. Against Lady Cindy a bagged Cheri Berry now reads "give Cheri Berry · answers 2 · +0.00"; before, nothing. Gated in tests/run.test.js, which pins that the FIGHT is what is priced — the same berry answers nothing against Youngster Calvin, a Rawst Berry answers nothing against Cindy because nothing there burns. Falsified: restoring the old filter turns it red.

findings.claim: Nothing in the platform knows a species' gender ratio. The fork's species table and upstream @smogon/calc both carry only gender 'N' for the genderless and undefined for everyone else, so a real gender cannot be derived for any Pokemon that has one.
findings.evidence: Checked both tables directly. profiles-side calc: Magnemite and Ditto come back gender "N", Jigglypuff, Piplup, Miltank, Tauros, Nidoran-F and Combee all come back undefined — including the two that are female-only. ai/node_modules/@smogon/calc answers identically, so this is not the fork having dropped it. genderRatio is undefined everywhere. The consequence is narrower than first written, because Attract is gender-independent here by design and does not need it. What still reads gender is Captivate (which does gate on it) and Cute Charm if [[cute-charm-gender-gate-undecided]] settles that way — both would behave as if every matchup were same-gender. rollIdentity does not author a gender and partySpecs does not forward one, so nothing owned ever carries one. Two routes if it is ever wanted, and the choice is Philip's: source a ratio table, or record it as an observed fact the way nature and ability already are, since gender is the most visible thing on a summary screen.

findings.claim: The documented Attract override is gender-independence for ATTRACT. Cute Charm shares the eligibility path and is therefore also gender-free, while the battle doc describes it as opposite-gender only. Both cannot be right.
findings.evidence: docs/AI_DATA_MODEL.md:700 describes the contact boundary as "Generation III+ Cute Charm infatuates a contacting opposite-gender attacker" — the vanilla rule. But Cute Charm applies infatuation through the same canApplyVolatile path as Attract, which carries no gender check, and model.test asserts a female holder infatuating female AND genderless attackers. docs/CONSTANTS-AUDIT.md:157 lists "gender-free infatuation at the eligibility layer" among honored R&B overrides, which would cover both; the profile flag is named attractIsGenderIndependent, which names only one. Raised as a question, not a defect, and deliberately not acted on: the last time this was treated as a defect it was a wrong call ([[attract-and-cute-charm-ignore-gender]]). Settling it needs either the hack's own documentation or ROM observation.

findings.claim: The upgrade list offers "Miracle Seed (pickup @ Route 104)" as a change to make for the fight ahead, and the panel gives you no button to take it. The split sheet carries the gate — "Route 104 · from #11" — and the advice row, which is where the player is told to act, does not.
findings.evidence: Eight occurrences across seven of eight scripted playthroughs, all reproducible: the driver read the row, went looking for the matching pickup button, and found none — seven for Miracle Seed and one for Silk Scarf. Both surfaces are deliberate and neither is wrong on its own. The advisor plans AHEAD: oracle.itemsObtainableBy(order) returns anything with opensAt <= the NEXT FIGHT's order, and tests/run.test.js asserts on purpose that a Grass Treecko should be told to go get the Seed before a fisherman at #22. The pickup list gates on PROGRESS: lib/run.js anchorOpen requires the guard fight (the earliest at order >= opensAt - 1) to have been beaten, and the same test asserts the Silk Scarf reads not-reachable at position -1. opensAt is "the first trainer at the location", so for the Seed at 11 that guard is Triathlete Mikey — the fight the upgrade is being priced FOR. So the advice is honest advice about a future fight and the button is honest about now; what is missing is that the advice row never says which. The detail string at lib/run.js:1398 is `${name} (pickup @ ${location})` with no gate, while the split sheet appends " · from #" + opensAt. Adjacent ruling, though it does not settle this one: egg-moves-ride-the-relearner — "The advisor may not offer what the bag cannot pay for." Deliberately not acted on; both behaviours are asserted on purpose and which one moves is a product call.

findings.claim: Best parties has two costs and the repo gates neither of the ones a player feels. Its shortlist adjudication is a flat ~5s at ANY box size, paid on every call; and its exhaustive C(box, 6) enumeration is free up to about 40 Pokemon and then runs away — 0.5s at 30, 4.2s at 42, 176s at 76.
findings.evidence:
CORRECTED, and the correction came from a gate that already existed. tests/run.test.js:262 asserts C(30,6) exhaustively — 593,775 combinations — inside a 5s budget, and it passes. My first reading of this said the cost IS C(box,6) and cited a driver whose per-fight wall clock went 36s to 120s as its box grew to 76. Measured properly, with rollouts:0 to isolate the enumeration from the adjudication that follows it:

  box  8 ·      28 combos · enumerate 635ms · with adjudication 5488ms
  box 12 ·     924 combos · enumerate 450ms · with adjudication 5335ms
  box 20 ·  38,760 combos · enumerate 833ms · with adjudication 5769ms
  box 30 · 593,775 combos · enumerate 1608ms · with adjudication 6050ms
  box 76 · 218,618,940 combos · enumerate 177,371ms · with adjudication 191,147ms

So two separate things. The adjudication is FLAT — 5.5s at a box of eight, 6.0s at thirty — which is the cost a player pays every single time they press Rank, at any box size, and nothing gates it because the existing test passes rollouts:0. The enumeration is genuinely combinatorial but does not bite until the box is large: at ~1.24M combinations a second it crosses the suite's own 5s budget at about box 42, and the gate stops at 30. A nuzlocke never gets there because one-per-route holds the box near ten; a level-caps run can roll an area again and reach 76 easily, which is how the driver found it. HALF OF THIS IS NOW GATED, and the finding no longer describes the repo. "Nothing gates it because the existing test passes rollouts:0" was true when written and is not now. tests/adjudication_cost.test.js, added in 83e8301, plays a real twelve- rollout adjudication and asserts a budget on it — in constructed calculator objects rather than in seconds, which is the instrument this repo settled on after three timing gates flaked on shared-runner load. So the flat cost a player pays on every Rank is pinned, and pinned in a unit that moves only when behaviour moves. The enumeration half stands exactly as described. tests/run.test.js:262 still stops at a box of 30 and the cost still runs away past about 42, so a box between those numbers is ungated and a box of 76 takes 177s. One thing measured since narrows who is exposed: the scripted driver never reaches it. A playthrough under --party=matrix logs zero rank: lines across a whole run, because the matrix board picks the six and rankParties is never called. This is a cost a HUMAN pays by pressing Rank with a large box, which is also why the object gate does not cover it — that gate measures one adjudication, and the ranker runs four. FIXED. The enumeration half is closed, and not by a ceiling: rankParties now keeps, per enemy column, the members that could win it and enumerates only those. The licence is the score itself — scoreSix is the sum over enemies of the best member in the six for that column, so a six is worth what its column winners are worth and a member that wins nothing is interchangeable. Measured against exhaustive over 27 fight/level pairs across the whole run at box 37 (2,324,784 combinations): the BEST SIX SCORE matched at every keepPerColumn tried, 27 of 27 even at four; the whole top-10 vector matched 19/24/25/25 of 27 at keepPerColumn 4/6/8/12; mean combinations 1,856/9,501/34,449/162,430. Default six is 245x less work with the optimum never wrong. Two errors found by measuring: cutting EVERY box turned C(7,6)=7 into one six and cost the diversity rows their reason to exist, so the cut now runs only above a million combinations (box 33) and every previously-gated box is untouched; and the star could be cut, which renames the overall best six as without-the-star, so it is now in the pool by construction. The cut is reported in a shortlist block and in the panel note rather than inferred, and exhaustive:true returns the whole box for the sacrifice question the cut is wrong for. Gate in tests/run.test.js was made to fail three ways: worst-per-column moves the best score, no threshold cuts a box of seven, a no-op cut enumerates all 1,947,792.

findings.claim: The roll authors a full identity — six IVs, a nature and an ability — hands it straight to the catch command, and shows none of it. A nuzlocke route gives one encounter, and the keep-or-flee decision was made blind to the part of it that was already decided.
findings.evidence: paintRoll printed species, level, method, encounter chance and a catch-odds quote. rolled.ivs, rolled.nature and rolled.ability were all in hand — run_panel.js:3113 passes exactly those into the catch command, and lib/run.js rollIdentity is documented as "the one author of a rolled Pokemon identity" so a client never invents them. They reached the box and the summary screen, one Pokemon at a time, AFTER the decision that depended on them. IV total is the one that matters most and it is measurable: a wild roll averages 93 of 186 while every trainer Pokemon is built with a flat 31 across the board, and the spread inside a single box runs about 56 to 130 — so the difference between the best and worst catch you own is nearly the size of the deficit to every opponent. At L21 that is 3-4 points in every stat, 5% of a Prinplup's HP and 10% of its Defence, landing on both sides of the exchange. FIXED: the card now carries "IV 118/186 · Adamant · Torrent" beside the odds. Gated in the browser against the catch that follows — a quote that drifts from what lands in the box is worse than no quote — and falsified by withholding the total, which reddens it.

findings.claim: The ranker spent 48 seeded rollouts — 78% of a fight cycle — adjudicating four candidate sixes that were near-duplicates of each other. It played the same team four times and called it four opinions.
findings.evidence:
Found while profiling where a fight cycle goes: /run/rank 78%, /run/advise 18%, /run/matrix 4%, and the battle engine itself 1% — a turn is 5ms, opening a fight is 10ms. Within rank, the exhaustive C(box,6) enumeration everyone would suspect is 5%; the other 95% is 4 parties x 12 seeded rollouts.

The cause is scoreSix: it scores a six by the best answer per enemy column, so swapping the member that answers nothing changes no column and no score. The shortlist it produces is therefore systematically near-duplicates. Measured over twelve fights with a fourteen-strong box and varied IVs: the top four ALWAYS shared five of six members and carried one identical grid score; all four adjudications returned the same pWin and the same eDeaths in eleven of twelve; and playing them reordered the top six ZERO times. Thirty-six of the forty-eight rollouts were replaying one team.

A first attempt at early elimination saved exactly nothing, and that is what exposed this: parties either won 12/12 or lost 0/12 together, so no party ever fell behind another far enough to stop. The degeneracy was the finding, not the optimisation.

FIXED: candidates are now picked for DISTANCE as well as rank — the best six, then the best that differs from every chosen one by at least two members. Same budget when four genuinely different sixes exist; fewer rollouts rather than repeated ones when they do not. Measured 4 adjudications down to a mean of 1.17, 48 rollouts to 14, /run/rank 11,275ms to 5,161ms, and a fight cycle from ~14.5s to ~8.9s. Gated on pairwise distinctness and falsified by adjudicating the first four regardless.

findings.claim: Every matchup cell computes a crit band for BOTH directions, and nothing reads the player-side one. The crit variant is a second Calc.Move and a second Calc.calculate per damaging move, 10,022 of the 25,975 objects an advise call builds.
findings.evidence:
Found while profiling the fight cycle. After the ranker fix the cycle is roughly /run/rank 5,161ms, /run/advise 3,081ms, /run/matrix 528ms, and advise builds 25,975 calculator objects — 12,549 at calc-adapter.ts:599 for the move being calculated and 10,022 at :784 for its crit variant, which runs a second full Calc.calculate. The cell keeps critMax for both sides; grepping lib/ and src/js/ finds consumers only for the THEIR side — run.js:1762 reads pairing.them.critMax, the matrix table renders `us` as min and `them` as crit, and the planning rule is stated as "their crit is what a plan has to survive, and our floor is what a plan may rely on".

DELIBERATELY NOT ACTED ON. planner.js:570 says in as many words: "Both travel with the cell so no consumer has to re-derive them from an average." That is a design statement about what a cell is, not an oversight, and the last time behaviour that looked redundant was "fixed" on inspection it was a declared rule and had to be reverted ([[attract-and-cute-charm-ignore-gender]]). Whether the player-side band is worth its cost is a product call: it is a real saving in the two hottest non-battle endpoints, against a cell contract that currently promises symmetry. FIXED. matchupDirection takes withCritBand and the player side passes false, so critCeiling never runs for us and the band is never built. Re-verified the claim first: zero reads of us.critMax, us.critKO, us.critMove or us.critPriority across lib, src/js, scripts and tests, against five reads of the them side. Three changes compound here — the engine memoizes calculateActionFacts and getEffectiveTypesForPokemon, and defers the crit band behind an accessor — so an advise grid went 25,975 objects at filing to 5,761 and then to 5,328 once our side stopped asking, 4.87x in total. The fields are omitted rather than zeroed, matching skipThem in the same file: a plausible number would be a quiet lie about a worst case, an absent one makes us.critMax / hp return NaN. Gate in tests/planner.test.js made to fail both ways: pricing our side again names the field, and dropping theirs says what a plan has to survive.

findings.claim: A single-use held item is modelled as permanent. Nothing removes it when it is eaten, so the run keeps crediting an effect that can never happen again and the advisor keeps pricing it.
findings.evidence: Give a Chople Berry to an Aron, beat Leader Brawly — whose team is more than half Fighting, which is exactly what makes a Chople Berry fire — and the Aron is still holding it afterwards while the bag reads {}. The only thing in lib/run.js that clears a held item is the unhold command at line 2897; beat does not touch items. The battle engine models consumption correctly (ai/src/berry-effects.ts, lastConsumedItem), so the berry IS eaten inside the fight — nothing writes that back to the run. Scarcity itself IS modelled: the bag decrements on give, and a second give is refused with "give: the bag has no Chople Berry", so one berry means one holder. It is only the eating that is missed. Not hypothetical. 162 of the 840 held items recorded across every report in ui-playthrough-out are Oran Berries — 19.3% — and an Oran Berry restores HP once and is gone. Every matchup after the fight that ate it has been pricing a heal that no longer exists. The data already knows the distinction and no code reads it: profiles/run-and-bun/oracle/availability.json tags each item with a kind, and grepping for "consumable" across lib, src/js and ai/src returns nothing. CORRECTION to this finding as first written: I said 116 of 194 entries carried no kind. That was wrong — the 116 are MAP entries in availability.json, not items. All 28 catalogued items do carry a kind. The real gap is narrower and sharper: only 28 items are catalogued for the whole game, no type-resist berry appears among them, and one of the 28 was misclassified — Focus Sash was tagged held while ai/src/move-engine.ts consumes it, so the run map itself described a one-shot item as permanent. Raised by Philip, who pointed out that an Eviolite is reusable and a resist berry is not, and that an advisor cannot price the two the same way.

findings.claim: The run map and the planning provider are built from independent transcriptions of Run & Bun's trainers, and they disagree about which fights exist. 148 of our 362 fights cannot be resolved in the provider at all, so those fights get no survival forecast.
findings.evidence: Traced from the forecast failures: after the evolution fix, 77 of the 101 remaining are "No unique canonical RAB trainer exists for X" rather than anything about abilities. The two lists are built independently. Ours comes from the setdex — planner.loadRunMap groups profiles/run-and-bun/encounters.js entries by trainer label — and holds 362 fights. The vendor holds 431, enumerable through createRabRunRuntimeProvider({}).options.resolveTrainer(order) for orders 1..434. resolveRabTrainerOrder demands exactly one exact-name match, so anything the two transcriptions name differently cannot be looked up. Measured across all 362: 210 resolve (58%), 4 are ambiguous in the vendor (the Elite Four, who appear twice for the rematch), and 148 fail. Of those 148, ZERO are formatting mismatches — normalising case and punctuation resolves none of them. 43 distinct names exist only in our map and 94 only in the vendor. Sequence alignment does not rescue it, and that was the plan worth killing. Both lists run in game order and the 210 anchors are strictly increasing, so aligning our gaps against the vendor windows looks obvious. It moves coverage from 58% to 63% and then stops, because the windows do not match the gaps: Bug Maniac James sits in a window with no vendor trainer in it at all, and Breeder Lydia in a gap of three against a window of one. Interpolation is worse than useless here in any case — an approximate order returns a DIFFERENT trainer's team, which is a confidently wrong forecast rather than an absent one. The disagreement is structural, not clerical. The vendor has "School Kid Jerry" alone at order 37; our map has "School Kid Jerry & Johnson", one fight against a double. Bug Maniac James, Twins Gina And Mia, Breeder Lydia and Breeder Isaac are absent from the vendor entirely. Our Team Aqua Grunts carry a location and an ordinal ("Museum #1"); the vendor has 24 entries all named "Team Aqua Grunt". So this cannot be fixed with a lookup layer, an alias table or a normaliser, which is what it looks like from the error message. It needs a decision about which database is authoritative for what the game contains, and a reconciliation — the same shape of work as provider-ability-table-is-vanilla-not-run-and-bun, and blocked the same way: the vendored package ships a bundled index.js with no trainer source to curate. CORRECTED AND FIXED, 2026-08-25, in the same day it was raised. The conclusion above — "this cannot be fixed with a lookup layer, an alias table or a normaliser" — was wrong, and it was reached before looking at what the engine actually stores. Philip suggested the failures were mostly double battles. They are, and that is the whole key. The engine files a DOUBLE under its lead and records the other half: order 37 is "School Kid Jerry", isDouble true, doublePartner "Youngster Johnson", four Pokemon. We write the same fight as "School Kid Jerry & Johnson" with the same four Pokemon. The names disagree and the TEAM does not, and a party of four to six species with levels turns out to be a fingerprint. Matching on it, with Mega and regional-form spellings normalised (beedrillmega against beedrill, avalugghisui against avalugghisuian — the normalisation alone took the match from 26 to 124): 124 of the 152 unresolvable fights get a unique engine trainer and ZERO get an ambiguous one. Coverage goes from 210 of 362 (58.0%) to 334 (92.3%), measured through the shipped browser bundle rather than in a fixture. It is safe because it is checkable against the answer already trusted: on the 210 fights the engine resolves by name, the team gives the same order 191 times and a different one never. The builder refuses to write a map if that ever fails. What the sequence-alignment paragraph above says still holds and is why this was not obvious: the two lists genuinely disagree about which fights exist, so aligning them by position stalls at 63%. Team matching does not care about position or about the 94 names that are only the engine's. It asks a different question. 28 fights remain unplaced and are refused rather than guessed, because an order that is off by one names a different trainer's team. Leader Flannery is among them, which makes this a genuine data gap rather than a naming one: Bug Maniac James, Breeder Lydia, Breeder Corgi, Breeder Isaac and Ranger Lydian have no counterpart in the engine at all, and Bird Keeper Perry & Chester is four Pokemon here against eight there. Shipped as profiles/run-and-bun/oracle/trainer-orders.json, generated by scripts/build-trainer-order-map.js from two pinned databases and consulted by scripts/entries/pokemon-provider-entry.mjs before the engine's own resolver. tests/trainer_orders.test.js rebuilds it, fails on drift, re-derives every team match from the engine, and pins that the unplaced stay unplaced. DUPLICATE, and an overstatement. provider-cannot-resolve-42-percent-of-the-run-map recorded this on 2026-08-21 with the same 152 of 362 count and the correct diagnosis, and I re-derived it from scratch today without finding it first. That one is the primary record and carries the fix. Worse, the claim above is wrong where the two differ. This finding says the databases "disagree about which fights exist"; the older one says the failures are "a naming convention, not missing content". The older one is right for 124 of the 152, which is exactly why matching on the team works — a naming disagreement leaves the team intact and a content disagreement does not. Only the remaining 28 are content, and they are the one thing this finding adds.

findings.claim: Neither engine performs Mega Evolution, and the two sides store opposite starting states for a Mega holder. The planning engine simulates the BASE form for the whole fight — 165 special attack modelled as 115 for Wattson's ace — while this run stores the evolved form, which is correct from turn one because evolution precedes move order, and only picks the enemy's first move a turn early. The divergence ledger cannot see any of it because the diff reads the species table, where the engine is correct, and never the trainer records, where it is not.
findings.evidence: Raised by Philip, who pointed out that the documentation should have abilities right and that some trainers hold abilities a player cannot. Both are true and neither is the bug. Trainers do exceed the player-legal set: 798 of the 1,624 trainer Pokemon in this run map (49.1%) carry an ability outside their own species list — Ferrothorn with Iron Barbs where the species allows Anticipation, Greninja with Protean over Torrent, Azumarill with Huge Power over Thick Fat. The setdex records those per Pokemon, so the run models them correctly, and rollIdentity reading the species table is right for a player catch. Comparing every enemy Pokemon the run and the engine both hold, 1,402 of 1,459 abilities agree. All but ONE of the 57 that differ are a Mega or Primal form, and the reason is not a wrong ability. It is a different starting state: ours {species: "Ampharos-Mega", ability: "Mold Breaker", item: "Ampharosite"} engine {species: "Ampharos", ability: "Static", item: "Ampharosite"} Both are defensible readings and neither survives the follow-up question. Grepping both sides for megaEvolve, megaStone, canMegaEvo and Mega Evolution returns nothing: NEITHER engine performs the evolution. So the two are not two spellings of one fight, they are two different fights. The engine simulates a plain Ampharos for the whole battle; we simulate the Mega from turn one; the game has the base form for one turn and the Mega for the rest. Ours is wrong for a turn. The engine is wrong for the fight, and by a lot — Mega Ampharos is 165 special attack against 115 and adds a Dragon type, Mega Aggron is 230 defence against 180, Mega Blaziken is 160 attack against 120. A forecast that plans around the base form is planning around a Pokemon the player never faces after turn one. 66 of 362 fights hold a Mega or Primal, 18.2%, and they are concentrated where it hurts: the leaders' aces, the rival, Maxie. 69 such Pokemon across the run. It is invisible to the drift check for a mechanical reason worth recording. DATA-DIVERGENCES.json holds 140 entries and NONE is a Mega, because scripts/diff-provider-data.js extracts the vendor species table with a regex over name/types/baseStats/abilities and pulls 1,367 species, of which zero are Mega forms — while the bundle plainly contains "Ampharos-Mega" with abilities ["Mold Breaker"], the correct value. The engine's species table is right. Its TRAINER records are what hold the pre-Mega state, and the diff never looks at those. So the engine has the data to be right and does not use it, and the divergence ledger cannot see the gap because it compares the wrong table. REFINED. "Ours is wrong for a turn" is true and too kind to us, because the turn it is wrong about is not wrong in a safe direction for every Pokemon. Our data is internally consistent and the representation is deliberate: 68 Mega species each holding the stone that evolves it, one Primal holding its Orb, and zero base forms holding a stone. The calculator handles it cleanly — Ampharos-Mega reads 131 special attack, 47 speed, Mold Breaker and Electric/Dragon whether or not the stone is in the item slot, so nothing is double counted and the stone is not doing hidden work. The error is confined to turn one, and its SIGN varies. Across the 45 distinct Mega and Primal forms the run holds: 25 are faster after evolving, so modelling the Mega from turn one overstates their speed, which is pessimal and safe. 14 have the same speed. But 6 are SLOWER as a Mega, and for those the pre-applied form understates the speed the player actually faces on the first turn — Ampharos-Mega by 10, Camerupt-Mega by 20, Garchomp-Mega by 10, Heracross-Mega by 10, Sableye-Mega by 30, Abomasnow-Mega by 30. That matters here specifically because the panel decides fights on a race — "you need 3 turns to KO, they need 2" — and breaks its ties on speed. For those six, the race verdict on turn one is computed against a Pokemon slower than the one that moves. Wattson's Ampharos and Maxie's Camerupt are both on that list, so it lands on leader aces rather than on filler. So the comparison is not "one turn wrong against a whole fight wrong". It is: ours is exactly right from turn two, safe on turn one for 39 of 45, and optimistic on turn one for 6 — a bounded, enumerable list. The engine is understated on every stat for every turn of all 45. Ours remains much the better approximation and the six are worth naming rather than rounding away. The cheap correction, if one is wanted without implementing Mega Evolution: the threat line already says what the enemy is, and for a stone holder it could say what it is UNTIL it evolves. That is a sentence, not an engine. CORRECTED BY PHILIP, and the correction removes the cost I had just finished measuring. Mega Evolution resolves BEFORE any move: both sides choose, the evolution happens, and then move order is decided by the EVOLVED Pokemon's Speed. So the pre-applied form gives the right Speed on turn one as well, including for the six that are slower after evolving, and the "optimistic on turn one for 6 of 45" paragraph above is wrong. Wattson's ace at 47 against a 47-Speed Prinplup is a genuine tie on turn one, not a panel error — and a model that used the unevolved 54 would be wrong from the opening turn rather than right. What the pre-applied form does get wrong is narrower and is a DECISION rather than a stat. On the turn it evolves, the enemy picks its move as the base form, because the choice is made before the evolution resolves — it does not yet know what it is about to become. It then executes that choice with the evolved stats, ability and types. Modelling the Mega from the start means our enemy chooses its first move from a Pokemon the real one has not become yet. The move is executed correctly; only the selection is early. That reorders the two errors rather than balancing them. Ours: every stat right from turn one, one enemy move choice computed a turn early. The engine: every stat of all 45 Megas understated for every turn of every fight, and Speed wrong from turn one in both directions. Ours is not a close call. The six slower forms are still worth naming, but as where the decision gap is visible rather than as an error list: a Pokemon that chose while fast and then moves slowly is exactly the case where choosing early looks different from choosing late. PICTURE COMPLETED, and the remaining gap turns out to cost nothing. Asked to model the turn-one decision as the base form, the first job was to size it, and the size is zero. The engine already has what such a change would need. state.firstTurnOutIds is maintained for Fake Out and First Impression and answers "is this its first turn out" exactly; speciesOverride and abilityOverride exist on PokemonState and the calc adapter honours them. So the change is tractable: at the AI decision point, if the actor is a Mega on its first turn out, evaluate with the base form and execute normally. Measured across all 69 Mega and Primal enemies in the run map, choosing as the base form picks a DIFFERENT move in 0 of them. Not a near miss either: in 0 of the 69 do the top two moves come within 25% of each other, so no reorder is close. A Mega scales its whole moveset at once and the ranking survives it — Wattson's ace reads Discharge 176 and Dragon Breath 67 as the Mega, and Discharge 132 against Dragon Breath 33 as the base form. Different numbers, same choice, and never close. That measurement needed two corrections before it meant anything, both of the kind that reads as a clean zero. The first compared action.kind, which is the literal string "move" for every action, so it was comparing a constant to itself. The second was a control that could not fail: overriding to Magikarp also picked Discharge, which looked like proof the override did nothing. It was not — Dragon Breath halves from 67 to 33 when the Dragon type goes away with the Mega form, which is the override working exactly as intended. The control was simply badly chosen, because Magikarp keeps Ampharos's moves and Discharge still wins them. So the recommendation is NOT to make the change. It would put a form-swap into the AI decision path — a core route under 485 tests, used by the driver and the planner alike — to alter no decision anyone can observe. The fidelity gap is real and it is inert. Bounded, because it is inert only against what is there now: the current AI scoring, and these movesets. A future Mega whose evolved typing makes a second move competitive would land inside that 25% band, and this is the measurement to re-run. NOT REPRODUCIBLE, re-measured 2026-08-26. The "0 of 69, and never close" that closed this out is wrong, and the reason it read as a clean zero is a FOURTH bad probe of the same family as the three already named above. calc-adapter keeps a CALC_POKEMON_CACHE keyed on state and Pokemon IDENTITY, and its docblock states the soundness argument plainly: nothing in the engine mutates a Pokemon, transition.ts only ever spread-copies. A probe that sets speciesOverride on a Pokemon IN PLACE and re-evaluates therefore reads the pre-edit Calc.Pokemon straight back out of that cache. Every damage number is identical, the choice never changes, and the zero is an artifact of measuring nothing. Verified: the same override on a freshly built state DOES move the numbers — Ampharos-Mega Dragon Breath 58 to 29 once the Dragon type goes, Discharge 78 to 57 on the lower special attack — and confirmed the cache is not something today's memo work introduced by reproducing the dead probe at 365de19, before either engine memo landed. The cache is CORRECT; the probe violated the invariant it documents. Re-run over deep COPIES, with the base species AND the base ability restored and the pre-applied Mega typing dropped, the damage moves for 69 of 69 and the first-move choice differs for THREE: Leader Flannery Charizard-Mega-Y Fire Blast to Air Slash, Aqua Admin Shelly Blastoise-Mega Surf to Shell Smash, Bug Catcher Davis Scizor-Mega Bullet Punch to Close Combat. One is a gym leader. The "no reorder is close" half does not survive either, but not in the direction it sounds: 61 of 69 have a TIED top score rather than a near miss — Winstrate Vicky's Medicham reads High Jump Kick, Zen Headbutt and Thunder Punch all at exactly 12.400 — so a 25% band measures how often the AI is indifferent, not how close it is to changing its mind. A flip between tied moves costs nothing by the AI's own metric, which is why the honest number here is three and not sixty-one. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE is the recommendation. Three of 69 Megas, in three of 362 fights, still does not buy a form-swap in the AI decision path. What changes is that "inert" was never established, so nobody should rely on it as settled: the gap is small, live, and now has three named cases to re-check against. Any future re-measurement must build copies rather than edit a Pokemon in place, or it will report zero again for the fifth time.

findings.claim: The field-item ledger published ENGINE trainer row indexes (0-434) into `opensAt`, which means run-map order (0-1620), under a `method` string that claimed run-map order outright. 160 of 164 dated rows were too early, by 591 on average and 1149 at worst.
findings.evidence: Leader Brawly is engine row 28 and run-map order 77; the builder never crossed that gap. Invisible to every gate because an engine index IS a valid run-map order, just a different fight. availability.json had carried both numbers side by side for every item the whole time — Soft Sand, Route 109, rabMinOrder 13 beside opensAt 29 — and the ledger published 185. Five further rules were wrong with it: "(Optionals)" is a fight category not a place, so Route 106 read 601 instead of its own first fight at 22; late-bias was applied ACROSS places as well as within one, so Oran Berry read 387 where availability.json says 0 and the Sitrus Berry was withheld until 804 when it grows on Route 110 at 230; a gate stated without the word "requires" was missed; "New Mauville" matched Mauville and was offered 206 orders early; and two trainers named Winstrate Vito stand 1020 orders apart. Both builder inputs were /tmp files and the builder had no entry point and no caller, so its docstring's claim that the test rebuilt it was false. Scale now comes from trainer-orders.json. The gate that catches it asserts the two independent imports agree about the scale: under the bug those pairs were out by 538%, 71% and 72%.

findings.claim: tests/item_locations.test.js, tests/run_api.test.js and tests/ability_reconciliation.test.js existed, were falsified, and were reported as part of a "495 pass" run while no npm script named any of them. The suite lists its files one by one and nothing noticed the new ones were missing.
findings.evidence: The count came from the suite; the confidence came from `node --test <file>` by hand; nothing showed the two were different claims. Wiring them in immediately failed ability_reconciliation, which still asserted entries.length > 0 from when 124 species contradicted — the upstream rebuild had taken it to 0 and the assertion had gone stale unnoticed. check-sdlc.js now refuses any tests/*.test.js that no `node --test` invocation names. The first version of that rule PASSED when broken, because it accepted a file listed for eslint as "run"; tightened, then made to fail twice (a test dropped from test:server but left in lint, and a brand-new unwired file).

findings.claim: Both order-scale gates asked `run.trainerIndexOf(doc, x) !== null` and called it a scale check. lib/run.js:687 SNAPS FORWARD to the first fight at or after x, so the only question it answers is "is x at most 1620". All 362 trainer numbers passed, and so did all 435 engine row indexes — the two scales those files exist to keep apart.
findings.evidence: Measured: trainerIndexOf(26)=11, (78)=27, (362)=99, (434)=118, (1620)=362, (1621)=null. Rewriting every dated row to its own trainer number left both files green — 56 of 56 moveItems rows and 186 of 186 ledger rows. Against the buggy ledger at d1a2d52 the assertion was green on 164 of 164 dated entries, which is the bug it was named for. AGENTS.md:67 claimed the file "fails if a dated row is ever written in trainer numbers"; it did not. Both now test membership in the 362 real fight orders (estimate.fightOrders()), which catches 103 of those 164 historical rows. Not complete either — 97 of the 362 trainer numbers are themselves real orders — so it is paired with the named per-row anchors, and AGENTS.md now says so instead of overclaiming.

findings.claim: Philip corrected Route 109 from play, 29 -> 42, because the route is post-Granite Cave and 29 put it before Route 107's own trainers, which run to 37. apply() rewrote only availability.entries — the strings `items` and `moveItems` did not appear in the script — so Soft Sand stayed at 29, and the item row is the one the advisor reads.

findings.claim: playerStateFromEntry fills a missing level with 100 and missing IVs with 31 across the board. A Pokemon caught without rolled IVs stores `ivs: {}`, so Object.assign({all 31s}, {}) plans it as a PERFECT-IV Pokemon. The bias is optimistic, which is the dangerous direction for a nuzlocke.
findings.evidence: Reproduced: run.apply({kind:"catch", species:"Poochyena", level:10}) stores ivs {}. Measured at level 30, zero EVs: unrolled reads 70 HP / 47 Atk / 35 Spe against 65/42/30 for an average roll and 61/38/26 for the worst — overstating HP and Speed by 5 against average and 9 against worst. Five points of Speed flips turn order, which flips a survival verdict. lib/battle-driver.js:588 already REFUSES a wild mon missing its rolled IVs ("roll the encounter once before fighting it"), so the repo answers the same question two opposite ways on two paths. The level default is separately reachable through POST /planner/predict, which accepts playerParty as raw JSON without running team.validate. The fix consistent with "a guess is worse than a gap" is to refuse, mirroring the species and moves refusals already at lib/planner.js:171-172. RE-DERIVED AND FIXED. Confirmed independently: run.apply({kind:"catch", species:"Poochyena", level:10}) stores ivs {}, and a Poochyena built at level 30 reads 70 HP / 35 Speed at the assumed-perfect spread against 65/30 average and 61/26 worst — the +5 and +9 the finding claims. Zero of the 4,860 Pokemon stored across every recorded run are missing a spread, so this was a latent bias rather than a live one, which is why fixing it had no blast radius. The fix is a SPLIT, and the first attempt was wrong. Flooring every missing IV to 0 broke two existing gates, because adviseCatches builds a prospect as {species, level, moves} with no ivs key and that shape went through the same function. A prospect is a different question: nobody has rolled it, and "is this worth catching" is asked at its best. An OWNED Pokemon with ivs {} is the one that must take the floor. The data already separates them — absent key versus empty object — so the split needs no new plumbing. Gated on the resulting HP rather than the ivs field, because the bridge omits IVs from the state when they equal its default of 31, so ivs undefined there MEANS perfect and reads like an absence. Owned-unrolled is 61, owned-perfect is 70, prospect is 70. Falsified both ways: restoring the perfect-fill fails one gate, and flooring prospects too fails three — the third being the two gates that caught the original mistake.

findings.claim: markBeaten's anti-loop guard is `return clicked ? next : null`, and act() ends in a bare object literal, so it is always truthy. findings.claim: The plan verdict prints a bare decimal — "contested by 0.1", "decided by 4.12" — with no unit, no scale and no legend. It is a gap between two AI action scores on the game's internal tuning scale, where a setup move is worth 6, and nothing on screen says so.
findings.evidence: Raised by Philip reading the panel: "what is contested by 0.1 or 4.12? What does this actually even mean? The unit is not clear." It is the gap between the enemy AI's best action score and its second best, on Run & Bun's own internal decision scale. planner.js:468 computes it as top.score minus runnerUp.score. The scale is the ROM hack's AI tuning, exported from ai/src/scoring.ts: a setup move starts at SETUP_BASE_SCORE 6, SETUP_INCAPACITATED_BONUS adds 3 when the target cannot act, a Weakness Policy partner scores 12, holding no item at all scores -20. So "decided by 4.12" is roughly two thirds of a whole setup move's baseline worth of preference, and "contested by 0.1" is the AI being all but indifferent between two moves. Neither of those readings is available to anyone looking at the panel. Measured across 490 planned fights: minimum 0, p25 1.4, median 6.4, p75 6.4, maximum 26.4. By band: 95 under 0.5, 45 between 0.5 and 2, 71 between 2 and 5, 241 between 5 and 10, 38 at 10 or more. The median sits almost exactly on one setup move, which is the closest thing to a natural unit the scale has. What is on screen is a bare decimal with no unit, no legend and no sense of what counts as large. A player cannot tell whether 4.12 is decisive or negligible, and the two words that carry it — "decided" and "contested" — sound like verdicts on the FIGHT rather than on the move choice. That misreading is the subject of plan-verdict-hides-a-dead-forecast, and 5689615 addressed half of it by appending the survival answer. The unit problem is the other half and is untouched: the number is now sitting next to a sentence anyone can read, which makes its own opacity more obvious rather than less. Not fixed here. Whether to name the unit, band it in words, or drop the number for a phrase is a product decision.

findings.claim: The heal rule could never fire at a wall: it required usHp <= 50 AND risk !== lethal, but risk=lethal means a crit kills, which against a 47% hardest hit is every HP under 50 — the firing window was the empty interval (47, 50]. Bayleef carried Synthesis into all nine Brawly attempts of skipwall4 A7 and pressed it zero times, including at 3% HP.
findings.evidence: skipwall4-A-calibration.json, report-skipwall4-A-7.json: 11 Bayleef attack-turns at <=50% HP across nine Brawly attempts, all under a lethal-class threat, zero Synthesis presses; the win (eval index 40) lost 5 of 6 on pure variance. Fourth instance of the lethal-clause family after status, speed drops (isolated 50-0) and screens. Gate: tests/playthrough_policy.test.js 'a heal fires when the healed body changes the fight' — failed before the fix, passes after; --heal-control=0 preserves the old gate as the A/B control arm.

findings.claim: The driver offered voluntary switches while the foe held Pursuit, which doubles on a switch-out and which the Run & Bun AI clicks on the prediction — a switch it kills hands over the exact KO the switch was meant to dodge. Raised by Philip after the skipwall4 A7 dig: the heal fix keeps a body alive in place, not in transit.
findings.evidence: brpursuit1 (6 pairs, skip-walls shared, revision 75bddbe, VALID, QC PASS both arms): control switched under a killing-Pursuit sentence 5 times in 170 sentence-turns, treatment 0 in 181 — the guard removes the event entirely. Tally null at this n (0/6 Brawly both arms): the addressable event is ~5 per 120 wall attempts, because most Pursuit deaths (85 vs 76 in the batch) are finisher ticks on bodies staying in at single-digit HP, which is the preservation problem, not the switch problem. Gates: battle-driver prices the doubled catch; policy refuses the switch only under the sentence; both failed first.

findings.claim: The first bank-bodies rule switched out every body (<=35% HP) the hardest hit could kill. brbank1 (8 pairs, skip-walls shared, revision 547ae1d, VALID, QC PASS both arms) falsified it: control beat Brawly 4/8, treatment 1/8; Gavi attempts won 13.1% vs 8.7%. Mechanism: 2.0 banks per Brawly attempt donated free hits and robbed 2.4 attacks (19.4 to 17.0 per attempt), foes downed fell 3.60 to 2.79, and our deaths were unchanged (5.94 vs 5.99) — the banked chips died on re-entry anyway. Preservation without a fight-ending clock buys nothing.
findings.evidence: Rule narrowed to the one case the diagnosis left standing: they act first AND the hit covers us, so the body dies before its attack either way and the conceded free hit costs nothing extra. The engine now prints " they act first" on the threat line (race.faster was computed and never shown). brbank2 (8 pairs, revision 45a047f, VALID, QC PASS) then falsified the narrowed rule too: foes downed per attempt 2.94 vs 2.67, deaths unchanged, Gavi attempts won 14.3% vs 9.6%. The faint grants a FREE ENTRY, a bank concedes a hit on the incoming body, so both versions trade a healthy body's hit for a chip that dies on re-entry. Retired to --bank-bodies=1 (default off) in 6ce1d3b. Preservation must happen in place: heals, screens, speed control.

findings.claim: decide() re-derived the same best move from the same view every turn with no rule watching whether the fight was moving. battery1 (the first headless scenario battery, post-Brawly documents) caught it: Aroma Lady Daisy at fight 79 went 1/20 with 17 fights hitting the 400-turn guard — Centiskorch pressed Fire Blast 342 times into a Florges that healed every chip back — and Bug Catcher Jose at 37 burned 130 turns a fight the same way.
findings.evidence: Fix: a progress clock on the foe lowest HP; ten turns without a new floor switches to a body the stall has not tried, bounded by the bench, never under a killing Pursuit. Measured on the same battery: Daisy 1/20 (17 stuck) -> 14/20 (4 stuck), Jose fights end in 20 turns instead of 130, all twelve healthy scenarios byte-identical. --stall-break=0 is the control arm.

findings.claim: Battle-state moves carry no PP fields — only a timesUsed counter nothing reads — so a move can be pressed forever and a mutual stall (healer vs chip) never ends. In the real game PP exhausts and Struggle ends the fight; the engine diverges exactly in the scenarios where the divergence decides the outcome (342 identical Fire Blasts in battery1).
findings.evidence: Probe 2026-08-28: state.sides.player.party[].moves = [{name}] at start, [{name, timesUsed}] after use; no maxPP, no decrement, no Struggle path observed. The stall-break policy rule works around the policy half; the engine half stands open. Fork rule check needed before modeling: whether Run & Bun alters PP at all.

findings.claim: Run & Bun guarantees three perfect IVs on the starter (operator ruling), and /run/identity rolled every scripted gift uniformly like a wild catch. The archive is the proof nobody noticed: across 72 banked runs, 59 starters had zero perfect IVs, 11 had one, 2 had two, none had three — the uniform distribution exactly, on the one body every run owns.
findings.evidence: Fix: rollIdentity({perfectIvs: 3}) picks the stats from the same draw stream (replay holds), /run/identity passes 3 for its whole scripted-gift class (starter, gift, static, trade — split the class if the hack does). Gates at lib and server level, both failed first. Measured at the gym walls via counterfactual starter-3iv (gymcf3): 0/30, 0/30, 1/30 — identical to baseline, because one corrected body does not move a six-death wall (whole-box max IVs moves Wattson to 15/30). The correction matters where the starter IS the run: the early game before the box fills, which the battery cannot price and the browser loop can. Every banked run predates the fix and keeps its recorded under-rolled facts.

findings.claim: The model gave the rival the Hoenn ace the PLAYER beats (vanilla Emerald friendly direction: Turtwig -> Swampert). Operator ruling: Run & Bun rival counters your pick (Turtwig -> Blaziken, Chimchar -> Swampert, Piplup -> Sceptile). Every run that declared a starter carried the wrong rival: wrong spine variants for every rival fight, wrong level-cap anchor trainers at the rival bosses (Cycling Road L38, Route 119 L66, Lilycove L73), wrong playbooks and matchup boards for those fights.
findings.evidence: Undocumented in the official 1.07 dump: Trainer Battles.txt lists all three variants of each rival fight with no selection rule, and Mechanic Changes.txt (read end to end) never states it — a direction error in careful data, unfalsifiable by any source the repo held. Fixed by ruling: STARTERS field renamed beats -> rival with flipped values; play.js, ask.js, template, panel follow; the direction pins in ask, play and browser_run failed against the corrected code first. Banked runs keep their recorded wrong rival as historical fact. Related sweep the same day: gift IVs are likewise undocumented everywhere (locations workbook scanned sheet by sheet, mechanics, AI doc, learnsets, tracker lua, public docs) — the starter 3-perfect rule and this direction are both operator rulings, recorded as such.

findings.claim: The run map was missing the game's first fight (the Route 103 rival trio) and pre-Wattson Mauville Wally. The coverage note had recorded both as undecidable — data loss or hack cut. The official 1.07 Trainer Battles document settles it: both exist in the game, so this data had lost them. Every date, cap, availability gate and display number sat on a scale three-to-five Pokemon short.
findings.evidence: Restored with a full-scale migration (+3 from the start, +2 more past old-206) across fourteen order-bearing stores, ~40 test pins in eleven files, and 240 banked run documents (position, skipped, orderScale stamp). The insertion surfaced two latent defects, both fixed in the same commit: the engine-row scan in build-trainer-order-map.js started at 1 against a 0-based database (row 0 is the rival's Treecko — the off-by-one was invisible exactly as long as the fight was missing from our side), and availability.json stores the HM gate twice (methods vs hmMoves) with nothing comparing the copies — surf slots opened five fights early for half a day mid-migration. tests/scale_consistency.test.js now gates membership, the twice-stored HM gate, label-derived LEVEL_CAPS and badge tiers, and engine row zero; each gate failed on injected drift before being trusted. The id-scale audit (workflow, 24 agents) that ran alongside is the standing inventory: rulings and stores that reference trainer LABELS survived the insertion untouched; every store of raw orders needed hand migration.
